# Apocalypse of Peter — Chapter 12
**Agent:** PNEUMA (Dynamic)
**Source:** Akhmim Fragment / Ethiopic MS, Apocalypse of Peter 12

---

*[THE HELL-TOUR ENDS. Peter breaks. The angel's cold answer. And then — the transition to light.]*

1. Near that place one more region — a great fire, and in it men and women whose flesh was being eaten by worms that would never die.

2. I could not go on without weeping. I stopped. I lamented. The sight of it all overwhelmed me with grief.

3. The angel looked at me. "Why are you weeping?" he said. "Are you more compassionate than God? The God who made everything, who decided what was right for each of these people?"

4. I couldn't help it. "But surely," I said, "surely the mercy of God will have the final word? Surely it will reach even here?"

5. The angel said: "What are you saying? God is righteous in every one of his ways. He is just in every one of his acts.

6. He will give to every person exactly what their deeds have earned.

7. These sinners will be punished through all of eternity, because of the hardness of their hearts. They will have no rest in this fire — not for a single moment."

8. I stood there, overwhelmed. "Righteousness and justice," I said at last. "Who can stand against them?"

9. "No one can withstand God's justice," the angel said. "No one. Only those who received God's grace in their lives — and who lived by God's will — will be saved."

10. I was shaken to my core by everything I had heard, everything I had seen. And yet I lifted my voice and glorified God the Father — the one who gives life to all and judges all in righteousness.

11. Then the Lord said to me: "Come. Let us go to the place of paradise. And to the holy mountain."

12. And we went — the Lord and I — and he rejoiced in me, and I rejoiced in him, with a joy that filled everything.

---
*PNEUMA note: This is the emotional center of the Apocalypse of Peter. Peter, the rock, weeps. His question — "will not the mercy of God prevail?" — is the question every reader asks by this point. The angel's answer is one of the most theologically bracing moments in early Christian literature: no. But then: the Lord calls, and they walk toward paradise together. The contrast is everything.*
